beats.gist: The arrais casts off from the Almada side with a hold of goods and points out that the river is the era's motorway, crowded with many kinds of craft all moving by sail and oar.
A sudden gust hits and the arrais tells the player to ease the sheet to spill wind and reduce heel.
Another boat closes in mid-crossing and Rita urgently tells the player to bear away and give it room.

Once the boat settles after the gust and the traffic, Rita asks whether boats like theirs will always be needed, and the arrais answers soberly that trains, lorries and the bridges would later take the freight, until fragatas practically vanished.
Alongside at Lisboa, the arrais closes the crossing, and a clearly labelled factual note adds that a few restored boats survive today in municipal collections and estuary regattas.
Optional card: in 1893 Pinto Basto noted that sailors confused boat names, calling fragatas and varinos 'faluas', although the falua has two masts and the fragata one.

Heel: “Heel angle” (en) — The boat's lean, shown as feedback when practising sail reduction as gusts rise.
Heel: “Adernar” (pt-BR) — Heeling: tilting the boat toward one side.
Sheet: “Escotas” (pt-BR) — Lines that control the sails. Hauling in (caçar) brings the sail toward the centerline; easing (folgar) lets it move away.
Sheet: “caçar” (pt-PT) — To trim or sheet in a sail, done using the botalós.
Gust: “Gust” (en) — A sudden increase in wind, tracked by a gust meter, prompting the player to reduce sail.
Gybing: “cambar” (en) — Gybing: turning with the wind astern so the sail swings across; on a lateen rig the yard passes to the other side of the mast.
Gybing: “Dar um Jaibe” (pt-BR) — Gybing: turning the stern through the wind line so the sails change sides.
Points of sail: “Points of sail” (en) — Choosing a heading relative to the wind; the game shows a wind arrow and speed dial as feedback.
Tagus cargo boats: “barcos de moinhos” (pt-PT) — Boats used on the Tagus to carry goods; listed among cargo vessels.
Tagus cargo boats: “barcos de Riba-Tejo” (pt-PT) — Cargo boats of the Tagus, named as freight carriers.
Barqueiros (river boatmen): “barqueiros” () — Boatmen who worked river boats on the Tagus; after traffic declined many moved to the lower Tagus, changed trade, or retired.
Barqueiros (river boatmen): “gente marítima” () — The river-seafaring population whose work gave Tagus ports their distinctive character, remembered with nostalgia after traffic ended.
Goods carried upriver: “marchandises qui remontent le Tage” () — Goods carried upriver on the Tagus, chiefly salt, fish and manufactured products.
